root_commitment.why: info binds the root and cannot stop it being minted. HPKE base mode is anonymous -- sealing needs only R_pub, which travels in the package -- so an attacker picks their own auth_root, signs a fabricated history under it, and wraps their own generation key to the GENUINE R_pub. Every signature verifies and the wrap opens. The published substituted-trust-root negative mutates info on existing ciphertext and never attempts this.
root_commitment.digest: RootCommitment = SHA-256( LP("done/pkg-root/v1") || LP(workspace_id) || LP(lineage_id) || LP(hex auth_root) )
root_commitment.sealed: beside R_priv in row 14's envelope, under the same recovery code
root_commitment.checked: recomputed from the manifest and compared BEFORE any generation unwrap

the_attackers_package.note: Internally consistent, and it opens. That is the point: the ciphertext is not the problem, and no amount of checking it helps. Only a value the attacker cannot seal separates this from a real package.

root_commitment.expected: the commitment differs, and the refusal happens before HPKE is exercised at all

construction.one_format: §14.2's cutover package, §14.4's terminal package and §9.3's fidelity archive are one format at §13.5's three lineage states — never-established, live, retired. §14.4 describes the service *populating the portable package* rather than producing a second artifact, and a live package is upgraded to a retired one by importing the terminal record
construction.manifest: Ed25519( assembler ; LP("done/pkg/v1") || LP(dec v) || LP(workspace_id) || LP(lineage_id) || LP(lineage_state) || LP(hex auth_root) || LP(hex lineage_head_digest) || LP(dec epoch) || LP(hex parts_digest) || LP(assembled_by) )
construction.parts_digest: SHA-256( LP("done/pkg-parts/v1") || for each part ASCENDING BY NAME: LP(name) || LP(dec count) || LP(hex digest) ). No separate part count: each part's count is already inside this digest, and a second field would restate it and could disagree with it
parts: checkpoint — row 7’s ciphertext and manifest. **Row 8’s attribution claims are inside it**, because they live in the content root, so there is no attribution part
epochs — enough signed authorization history to resolve credential to capability at any referenced epoch (§14.2 item 2)
suffix — envelopes after the checkpoint, to row 6’s depth
generations — the historical content keys, wrapped (§14.2 item 4)
head — the signed live head, or the signed terminal record (§14.2 item 5, §15 row 9)
recovery — R_pub and the code-sealed R_priv (row 14)

trust_root_anchor.info: LP("done/gen-wrap/v1") || LP(workspace_id) || LP(lineage_id) || LP(hex auth_root) || LP(dec gen), as HPKE base-mode info
trust_root_anchor.why: §14.2 requires the old trust root *bound so it cannot be substituted*. Every other link in the chain is service-signed, so a forger supplying their own root can re-sign all of it; the chain has to terminate in user-held material, and the recovery code is the only such thing. Binding the root in the wrap's `info` means a substituted root opens no generation, so there is no content to re-attribute
trust_root_anchor.why_info_not_aad: `info` is never transmitted. A reader must supply the root it believes rather than read one out of the package, so a wrong belief fails to open instead of failing to match
trust_root_anchor.granularity: Per generation, which §14.1 makes correct rather than convenient: migration rotates to a fresh generation under the new lineage, so pre-migration generations stay anchored to the root that was in force when they were written
trust_root_anchor.never_established: §9.3’s Local archive has no lineage, so the lineage field is empty and `auth_root` is the archive identity’s own digest — SHA-256 over LP("done/archive-root/v1") || LP(hex archive_pub) || LP(hex archive_sign_pub) — committed under the code beside both private halves (`S0-6` return, `FU-02`). What authenticates a Local archive is the code that opens it, for the manifest as well as the wraps: the signing half verifies the manifest, the encryption half opens the generations, and neither authority is resolvable from anything the package alone offers. The archive still answers *does ciphertext still exist* for a holder without the code

local_archive.why: The S0-9 conviction (FU-02/A-04/ST-01): the factor sealed an HPKE recipient while a separate device key, never bound by the factor, authenticated the manifest — so a fresh wrap to the genuine public archive_pub could open an independently chosen generation key under a fabricated manifest. The identity now has two halves under one code, and the composed importer refuses the fresh mint at the commitment, before its signer is consulted and before any unwrap.
local_archive.identity: X25519 archive_pub/archive_priv opens the wraps; Ed25519 archive_sign_pub/archive_sign_priv signs the manifest. One identity per workspace (P-6), minted at first archive, retired to legacy at promotion.
local_archive.auth_root: SHA-256( LP("done/archive-root/v1") || LP(hex archive_pub) || LP(hex archive_sign_pub) ) — in the manifest slot a lineage’s trust root would fill, so the commitment formula and the wrap info are unchanged and one importer serves all three lineage states
local_archive.envelope: K_archive = HKDF-SHA256(ikm = utf8(code), salt, info = LP("done/archive/v1") || LP(workspace_id)); ct seals archive_priv || archive_sign_priv || RootCommitment under AES-256-GCM; AAD = LP("done/archive/v1") || LP(workspace_id) || LP(dec v) || LP(hex archive_pub)
local_archive.aad_note: The AAD binds the encryption half so the sealed private halves cannot be offered beside somebody else’s public key. The signing half is bound through auth_root inside the sealed commitment instead, deliberately: the commitment is the one value the attacker cannot seal, and keeping it the sole carrier of the signing identity is what lets the fresh-mint negative isolate it.
local_archive.importer: One path, §5’s order: the code opens the envelope; the sealed commitment is checked against the manifest before anything the package says is trusted; the manifest verifies only under the committed signing identity — never under a key the package offers; the parts digest is checked; only then are generations unwrapped.

terminal_handoff.why: The S0-9 conviction (FU-03/A-05): catchup_digest was SHA-256 over two public heads beside a bare count, so a stale receiver could self-assert completeness and authorize hosted destruction. The digest now commits the full bytes of a signed CatchupTranscript, and the gate verifies the transcript itself.
terminal_handoff.receipt: H = LP("done/handoff/v1") || LP(dec v) || LP(workspace_id) || LP(lineage_id) || LP(hex terminal_head_digest) || LP(hex retired_package_digest) || LP(receiver_credential) || LP(hex receiver_prior_head) || LP(hex catchup_digest) || LP(dec known_absence_count); sig = Ed25519(the receiving client’s signing credential; H)
terminal_handoff.transcript: T = LP("done/catchup/v1") || LP(dec v) || LP(workspace_id) || LP(lineage_id) || LP(dec source_epoch) || LP(dec link_count) || for each link: LP(hex prior) || LP(hex head) || LP(dec absence_count) || for each: LP(absence_id); sig_T = Ed25519(the lineage’s certification in force at source_epoch; T); catchup_digest = SHA-256(T)
terminal_handoff.authority: The transcript’s verifier resolves from the lineage’s client-authenticated certification in force — an input, never a key read out of the answer (FU-06’s rule at this gate). The receiver’s own credential can never fill it, so neither actor signs both parts of the receipt.
terminal_handoff.verified_current: Two forms and neither is a timer: the receiver’s accepted head is the terminal head and catchup_digest is empty, or the receipt commits a transcript that verifies under the certification in force, chains link by link from the receiver’s authenticated prior head to the terminal head, and enumerates every known absence by identifier — with the count the receiver signed equal to the list the transcript carries.

deletion_authority.why: One gate, one domain (P-4 falsifier 17, the S0-7 return): this gate and the retention model state the same predicate over the same six classes, and scripts/check-retention.mjs cross-checks this published statement against §14.7’s table and the executable model — drift in the class list or the time semantics fails a build rather than passing both. The five-entry copy that omitted recovery-anchor died here.
deletion_authority.before_the_boundary: a class deletes only with a durable per-class TerminalHandoff — S0-6’s gate, untouched
deletion_authority.destructive_boundary: retired_at + RETENTION, written exactly once at the cause overwrite and never earlier than an inherited deadline
deletion_authority.at_the_boundary: erasure executes the owner’s intrinsic acceptance, carried in the signed retire payload, and terminates in deleted-without-receipt — a terminal state no reader can take for a receipt; elapsed time is never an authority

transcript.signed_by: the lineage’s certification in force — modeled by k_auth

construction.hpke: RFC 9180 base mode, DHKEM(X25519, HKDF-SHA256) / HKDF-SHA256 / AES-256-GCM (row 1). Implemented in the generator rather than pinned as a string, because this row’s claim is a binding inside it; it reproduces RFC 9180 A.1.1 on every invocation before it is used

not_here.primitives: SHA-256, HKDF, AES-256-GCM, Ed25519 and X25519 KATs are row 1’s.
not_here.checkpoint: The checkpoint and its manifest are row 7’s.
not_here.attribution: The claims inside the checkpoint are row 8’s.
not_here.recovery_seal: The code-sealed R_priv envelope is row 14’s, unchanged by this row.
not_here.suffix_depth: How deep the suffix part reaches is row 6’s.

k_auth.role: The vanished service's authorization signing key — §14.2's trust root, and the thing this row exists to bind. It also signs a terminal package's own manifest.

forged_root.role: A forger's own authorization key, offered in the trust root's place so the substitution is a value rather than a description.

laptop.role: The restoring credential, which assembles a live cutover package and signs its manifest.

recovery.role: The account recovery keypair. `R_pub` wraps every generation; `R_priv` is what row 14's code opens, and it is where this row's anchor terminates.

vectors.name: live-cutover-package
vectors.why: §14.2’s package: the old service is unreachable and a restoring laptop carries the workspace to a replacement. Everything §14.2 enumerates is a part, and the fifth thing row 9 added — the old lineage’s signed head — is the `head` part.

vectors.name: retired-terminal-package
vectors.why: §14.4’s package, which is the same artifact after the service committed a terminal record: `lineage_state` moves to retired, the `head` part becomes that record, and the service signs the manifest because it is the assembler. Nothing else about the format changes, which is the claim this row makes.

vectors.name: never-established-archive
vectors.why: §9.3’s fidelity archive of a Local workspace, which is §13.5’s third lineage state rather than a fourth artifact. No epochs, no head, no suffix and an empty lineage; the archiving device is the assembler, and **what authenticates it is the code that opens it** — now for the manifest too (`S0-6` return, `FU-02`): `auth_root` is the digest of both public halves of the factor-sealed archive identity, the manifest verifies only under the committed signing half, and the composed importer is run over exactly this published package.

truncation_moves_the_parts_digest.why: A real truncation changes a part’s count and therefore the digest that binds it. It is published as a demonstration rather than as an isolating negative because it changes two things at once, and a negative that changes two things tests neither.

must_fail.name: substituted-trust-root
must_fail.mutate: Open a generation wrap while claiming the forger's authorization key as the trust root. **This is the row.** §14.2 requires the root *bound so it cannot be substituted*; binding it in the wrap's HPKE `info` means a substituted root derives a different key schedule and the wrap yields no content key — so a package with rewritten history has nothing to rewrite it over.

must_fail.name: substituted-lineage
must_fail.mutate: Open a generation wrap under another lineage identifier. A migration establishes a new lineage rather than succeeding the old one (§14.1), so a wrap must not carry across one.

must_fail.name: wrap-from-another-workspace
must_fail.mutate: Open a generation wrap as though it belonged to another workspace.

must_fail.name: wrap-of-another-generation
must_fail.mutate: Open generation 3’s wrap claiming generation 2. The binding is per generation because §14.1 rotates forward at migration, so old generations stay anchored to the root in force when they were written.

must_fail.name: retired-presented-as-live
must_fail.mutate: A retired package’s manifest presented with `lineage_state` reading `live`. §14.4 lets an offline replica keep a stale **live** head and forbids it claiming to have observed retirement; hiding a retirement that the package does carry is the same rule pointed the other way.

must_fail.name: substituted-lineage-head
must_fail.mutate: A manifest whose lineage-head digest is changed while everything else stands. This is the field row 9 added to §14.2’s list, and it is what stops a restoring device having to ask a replacement service where the old lineage stood.

must_fail.name: parts-digest-substituted
must_fail.mutate: The parts digest replaced, with no part changed. Isolates the field; the demonstration below is what a real truncation does to it.

must_fail.name: assembled-by-another-credential
must_fail.mutate: A well-formed manifest signed by a different credential. The assembler is named in the message, so this fails on the binding and not only on the key.

must_fail.name: manifest-wrong-workspace
must_fail.mutate: Verify the manifest against another workspace.

must_fail.name: manifest-wrong-lineage
must_fail.mutate: Move the manifest to another lineage.

must_fail.name: manifest-substituted-trust-root
must_fail.mutate: The manifest’s own trust-root field changed. The signature half of the anchor: the wrap makes a substituted root useless, and this makes it detectable before anyone tries.

must_fail.name: manifest-wrong-epoch
must_fail.mutate: Move the manifest to another epoch number.

must_fail.name: manifest-wrong-version
must_fail.mutate: Claim manifest version 2 for a version-1 manifest.

must_fail.name: freshly-minted-package-under-an-attacker-root
must_fail.why: The attack `substituted-trust-root` cannot reach, and the reason this row needed reopening. HPKE base mode is anonymous: the attacker needs only R_pub, which travels in the package. So they pick their own auth_root, sign a fabricated history under it, and wrap their OWN generation key to the GENUINE R_pub with info naming their own root. Every signature verifies, under a root they minted, and the wrap opens -- nothing in the ciphertext is wrong. What refuses it is the root commitment sealed beside R_priv, which the attacker cannot produce without the code.

must_fail.name: attacker-root-refused-before-any-unwrap
must_fail.why: Order, not just outcome. The commitment is checked against the manifest before a single generation is unwrapped, so a package whose root is wrong is refused without exercising HPKE at all. An implementation that unwrapped first and checked afterwards would still have opened attacker-chosen content before noticing.

must_fail.name: root-commitment-for-another-lineage
must_fail.why: The commitment binds all three fields, so a genuine commitment from one lineage does not authenticate a package claiming another.

must_fail.name: archive-under-a-wrong-code
must_fail.why: The archive identity is sealed under the code and nothing else. A wrong code opens neither keypair nor the commitment beside them, which is what "the code that opens it" has to mean once it is a construction rather than a sentence.

must_fail.name: archive-envelope-repaired-with-another-identity
must_fail.why: Row 14's own negative, at the archive: an envelope presented alongside a public key that is not the one it was sealed for. The identity is in the envelope's AAD, so the pairing is authenticated rather than assumed -- without it, an archive's sealed private half could be offered beside somebody else's public half.

must_fail.name: aad-only-archive-envelope-workspace
must_fail.why: The AAD's workspace binding, isolated from the key derivation's. The HKDF info binds the workspace too, so a negative that changed both would be rescued by neither; this one opens with the genuine derived key and an AAD claiming another workspace, so only the AAD can refuse it.

must_fail.name: aad-only-archive-envelope-version
must_fail.why: The envelope version, bound so a v1 envelope cannot be presented as a later one whose rules differ.

must_fail.name: aad-only-renumbered-archive-label
must_fail.why: The construction label, the same discipline as every other AAD here.

must_fail.name: freshly-minted-archive-under-an-attacker-root
must_fail.why: The account path's fresh-mint attack, at the state S0-9 convicted (FU-02/A-04/ST-01). HPKE base mode needs only archive_pub, which travels in the archive; Ed25519 verification needs only the signing key the manifest names, and the attacker names their own. So the package is internally consistent end to end -- its wrap round-trips under the genuine archive scalar and its manifest verifies under the signing key its auth_root commits, both asserted before the negative runs. Only the commitment sealed under the code separates it from a real archive, because the attacker's auth_root commits a signing identity the factor never sealed.

must_fail.name: archive-refused-before-any-unwrap
must_fail.why: Order, observed rather than inferred, exactly as the account path observes it: the commitment is checked before the manifest signer is consulted and before a single generation unwrap runs, so an attacker-rooted archive is refused without opening any attacker-chosen content.

must_fail.name: archive-manifest-signed-by-the-archiving-device
must_fail.why: The pre-return world, kept as the permanent negative (FU-02): the shipped positive verified the archive manifest under the laptop's device key, an authority the archive factor never bound. Here the device's signature over otherwise-genuine fields -- genuine, and asserted to be -- is refused, because the manifest verifies only under the signing identity the sealed commitment carries, never under whatever key the package offers.

must_fail.name: archive-signing-identity-not-committed-by-the-root
must_fail.why: The second door the same conviction opens, closed by the same resolution rule: keep the genuine auth_root so the commitment agrees, and present your own signing key beside it. The manifest signer must be the identity the commitment-checked auth_root itself commits, so a signing key the root does not derive verifies nothing -- however genuine its signature, and that it is genuine is asserted first.

must_fail.name: archive-parts-not-the-manifests
must_fail.why: The composed importer checks the parts against the manifest the factor-committed identity signed, on the Local path -- the check the pre-return isolated opener never made, because it never met the manifest at all.

must_fail.name: archive-wrap-from-another-workspace
must_fail.why: The generation wrap binds the workspace, so an archive of one Local workspace opens no generation of another. The envelope and manifest agree with the mutated workspace on purpose -- sealed and signed for it -- so the refusal is the wrap’s alone rather than one check wearing four hats.

must_fail.name: archive-wrap-of-another-generation
must_fail.why: And the generation, for the same reason.

must_fail.name: live-manifest-relabelled-as-retired
must_fail.why: Row 10 said a live package is UPGRADED to a retired one by importing the terminal record, and not replaced. There was never an upgrade to verify: lineage_state is inside the message the assembler signs, so relabelling it leaves a signature that no longer covers what it names. This is that claim, executed -- the honest live signature against a manifest calling itself retired.

must_fail.name: retired-manifest-under-the-assembling-credential
must_fail.why: And the other direction. A complete retired package is signed by the terminal authority, so it does not verify under the device that assembled the live one -- which is what makes "complete package" mean something rather than being a label on the same bytes.

must_fail.name: deletion-without-a-handoff
must_fail.why: The gate. No hosted class is destroyed on an elapsed window, a request, or a terminal record the service wrote itself. Something a receiver signed has to exist first.

must_fail.name: handoff-from-a-receiver-behind-the-terminal-head
must_fail.why: A receiver whose accepted head is not the terminal head is not current, and saying so is the whole point -- otherwise 'verified-current' means 'was reachable recently'. It may still qualify, but only by presenting a transcript.

must_fail.name: catchup-of-public-endpoints-alone
must_fail.why: The pre-return acceptance, kept as the permanent negative (FU-03/A-05). catchup_digest used to be SHA-256(LP(priorHead) || LP(terminalHead)) -- two public values any stale receiver can hash -- beside a bare count, so the actor whose completeness was in question could self-assert it. That exact receipt, digest and knownAbsences: 0 and all, is now refused: a digest with no transcript behind it commits nothing.

must_fail.name: handoff-with-an-unverifiable-catchup
must_fail.why: A receipt whose catchup_digest does not commit the transcript presented beside it. The receiver signed for verifying one thing and is showing another, and the gate reads only what the signature covers.

must_fail.name: catchup-transcript-signed-by-the-receiver
must_fail.why: The self-assertion attack with a real transcript: the stale receiver writes its own catch-up and signs it with its own credential. The signature is genuine -- that is asserted before the negative runs -- and it verifies under nothing the gate consults, because the transcript's verifier resolves from the lineage's certification in force, never from the answer (FU-06's rule, at this gate).

must_fail.name: catchup-transcript-not-from-the-prior-head
must_fail.why: A genuinely signed transcript that chains from somewhere else. Without links[0].prior bound to the prior head the receiver authenticated, any transcript would do, and the catch-up would be a formality.

must_fail.name: catchup-transcript-with-a-broken-link
must_fail.why: An interior link that does not name its predecessor. A chain proof is only a proof at every link; a gap in the middle is the same unreceived content as a gap at the ends, wearing continuity.

must_fail.name: catchup-transcript-short-of-the-terminal-head
must_fail.why: A genuinely signed transcript that stops before the terminal head. Caught up to almost the end is behind, and a receiver that verified it is not current in either of the two forms the gate accepts.

must_fail.name: handoff-with-unenumerated-absences
must_fail.why: The pre-return positive's own numbers, kept as the detected negative: a count of two beside an empty list. 'Some updates could not be recovered' is not a known-absence list, and a deletion authorized on it destroys the only copy of what was never enumerated. The count the receiver signs must equal the list the transcript carries.

must_fail.name: catchup-absence-without-an-identifier
must_fail.why: An absence entry that names nothing. The count-to-list check alone would accept two empty strings as two absences, so each entry must be an identifier -- the gaps are named rather than counted.

must_fail.name: handoff-for-another-retired-package
must_fail.why: The receipt binds the exact package digest, so acknowledging one retirement does not authorize deleting the bytes of another.

must_fail.name: handoff-signed-by-a-non-receiver
must_fail.why: The receiver is named in the message, so a service that can assemble the package cannot also sign for having received it.
